rewrite.question: An HTTPS page references a script and an image over plain HTTP. What do current browsers do, and why?
options: Both load normally, since only the page's own HTML is protected
The script is blocked and the image is upgraded to HTTPS, because an HTTP subresource can be altered on the path
Both are blocked, because an HTTPS page may never issue an HTTP request
Both load but are marked insecure, leaving the decision to the user
rewrite.hint: A script can rewrite the whole page; an image cannot. Would a browser treat the two the same way?
rewrite.explanation: An HTTP subresource can be read and rewritten by anyone on the path, and a rewritten script owns the page, so browsers block mixed scripts, stylesheets, iframes and fetch requests outright. Images, audio and video are auto-upgraded to HTTPS instead, and blocked if the upgrade fails or the URL names a bare IP address. The everyday consequence today is therefore a broken page rather than a silent compromise - but the reason for the block has not changed, and serving every subresource over HTTPS is still the fix.

rationale: The threat model is right but the browser behavior it implies is years out of date, which is the kind of staleness that misleads a learner debugging a real console error.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Mixed_content (browsers auto-upgrade image, video and audio mixed content requests from HTTP to HTTPS and block insecure requests for all other resource types; upgradable requests are blocked when the host is an IP address)
